questions.q: What was the exact date on which Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly, and what was the immediate outcome of that session?
questions.a: Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946; it was adopted unanimously on 22 January 1947 after a week of debate. A wrong answer (e.g., citing 1947 or 1950) reveals the student confuses the Resolution's adoption with Independence or Constitution commencement dates, indicating a lack of chronological anchoring in the constitution-making timeline.

questions.q: The Objectives Resolution uses the phrase "justice, social, economic and political." Explain why the framers deliberately listed three distinct types of justice instead of just writing "justice."
questions.a: The threefold classification responded to the freedom movement's realization that political freedom (vote) alone was insufficient without economic redistribution (land reforms, labor rights) and social dismantling of caste/gender hierarchies. A student who answers "justice means fairness" shows only a dictionary understanding, missing the historical specificity that each adjective maps to a distinct set of constitutional provisions (e.g., social justice → Art. 15-17, economic justice → Art. 39, political justice → Art. 326).

questions.q: A student argues: "The Objectives Resolution was just a speech; it had no legal force because it wasn't a law." Using the Constituent Assembly's own procedure, explain why this argument is constitutionally incorrect.
questions.a: The Resolution was adopted as a formal resolution of the Constituent Assembly, which functioned as both legislature and constitution-making body. Its principles were explicitly incorporated into the Preamble (which the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati held is part of the Constitution's basic structure) and guided every subsequent committee's work. A wrong answer indicates the student misunderstands the dual role of the Assembly and the concept of "constitutive power" versus ordinary legislative power.

questions.q: Compare the Objectives Resolution's safeguards for "minorities, backward and tribal areas, and depressed classes" with the Preamble's phrase "fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation." What shift in constitutional language does this reveal?
questions.a: The Resolution names specific vulnerable groups requiring affirmative protection, while the Preamble elevates the goal to a universal principle of fraternity that binds all citizens. This shows a shift from group-based protective language to a unifying normative ideal, without dropping the substantive safeguards (which appear in Arts. 15-17, 29-30, 46, etc.). A student who sees them as identical misses the rhetorical and juridical evolution from "safeguards" to "fraternity."

questions.q: Critique the view that the Objectives Resolution was merely a reflection of Nehru's personal socialism. Use evidence from the Constituent Assembly debates to support your evaluation.
questions.a: The Resolution was drafted by a sub-committee (Nehru, Patel, Prasad, Azad, etc.), debated for six days with 30+ speakers including Ambedkar, K.M. Munshi, and socialist members, and adopted unanimously. Amendments from the right (property protection) and left (explicit socialism) were both rejected in favor of the consensus wording. A student attributing it solely to Nehru ignores the collective deliberative process documented in CAD Vol. I, revealing a "great man" history bias rather than institutional history.

questions.q: Draft a one-sentence "Objectives Resolution" for a hypothetical student council constitution that mirrors the Indian Resolution's structure: sovereignty source, three-dimensional justice, liberties, and safeguards for vulnerable groups.
questions.a: A strong answer: "This Council derives its authority from the student body, pledges social, academic, and disciplinary justice, guarantees freedom of expression, association, and fair hearing, and ensures representation for first-year, minority-community, and differently-abled students." A weak answer omits one dimension (e.g., only "justice" without adjectives) or copies the Indian text verbatim without adapting to the school context, showing inability to abstract the structural template.
